criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1: The paper examines strategic utility-level sustainability, resilience, circular economy, wastewater treatment technology, and aging pipe infrastructure in Finnish urban water management rather than household or community water or sanitation service access (explicitly noting that universal access under SDG 6 is not a major problem in Finland).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, the paper discusses broad governance, institutional frameworks, municipal responsibility for service provision, utility autonomy, and cost-recovery/profit principles under the Finnish Water Services Act. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, it fails because these appear only as broad, unanalysed macro-governance background in a strategic utility PESTEL/SWOT overview rather than a specific rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3: The article reports no primary empirical data (no sample, respondent counts, utility dataset, or empirical estimates) and is not a systematic empirical synthesis (no search strategy, screening criteria, or systematic extraction). Instead, the first author performs a narrative synthesis and desktop PESTEL/SWOT brainstorming exercise summarizing conclusions and notes from four of his own earlier publications and doctoral thesis.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: No household or community outcome related to access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion is measured or reported; the stated target outcome is a conceptual framework and SWOT matrix for sustainable and resilient urban water services from a water utility perspective.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails Criterion 5: No empirical study population, sample size, or unit-level empirical exposure-outcome design is reported in the text.
criterion_notes.c6: Passes Criterion 6: Full text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: According to the United Nations’ SDG 6 Clean Water and Sanitation initiative, proper water services will be provided for everyone by 2030, with special attention to be paid to women, girls, and those living under vulnerable circumstances. While not a major problem in Finland, this is a huge challenge globally.
Water utilities produce the services [1]; hence, water utilities are relatively independent, and they do their own annual accounting, while their operation and economics are regulated by law.

The material for this study was collected from previous studies focused on Finnish water services [26–29]. The data were collected using literature reviews, questionnaires, interviews, and different analyses (e.g., life cycle assessment (LCA) and economic viability analysis) for making conclusions from the raw data. To summarize the results, a sequential PESTEL and SWOT analysis was carried out.

The outcome that was targeted in the objectives of this study was “Sustainable and resilient urban water services”. Pillars that support and have an effect on this outcome are illustrated in Figure 3.
Deteriorating water pipe and sewer networks and treatment of harmful substances are the main weaknesses in Finnish urban water management at the moment.

raw_response.exposure: Macro-level political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal (PESTEL) factors in Finnish urban water utility management
raw_response.outcome: Conceptual SWOT matrix of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats for sustainable and resilient urban water utilities (no empirical service access outcome reported)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E05 (no empirical evidence; also fails c1, narrow c2, c4, and c5). This article is a narrative synthesis and first-author strategic PESTEL/SWOT brainstorming overview drawing on four of the author's previous Finnish water-sector studies and PhD dissertation, presenting no primary empirical data, sample description, or systematic review methodology. Furthermore, it focuses on utility-level asset management, wastewater treatment, and institutional resilience rather than household or community service access, and reports no access-related empirical outcomes; therefore it is excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain reading of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Non-empirical narrative synthesis and desktop sequential PESTEL/SWOT strategic overview of prior studies
